result:
There's a library I keep thinking about that doesn't exist.

It's not a library of books that were published. It's a library of unfinished things.

Half-knitted sweaters where the maker got bored or got better at knitting and decided to start over. Novels abandoned on page 73. Duolingo streaks that died at 41 days. Gardens that were enthusiastically planted in May and quietly surrendered to weeds by July. Business plans scribbled on napkins. The sourdough starter someone named "Bubbles" that lived in the back of the fridge for six months.

If you walked through it, you wouldn't feel like a failure. You'd feel *relief*.

Because every shelf would prove the same quiet truth: everyone starts more things than they finish. Curiosity is wider than discipline, and that's not a flaw. That's how you're supposed to be built.

We treat finishing as the only honorable outcome, but starting is its own kind of courage. To start something is to say, "I don't know how to do this yet, but I'm willing to look silly for a while." Most people never even do that.

The most interesting people I know — or have read about, or imagined — aren't finishers of everything. They're serial starters. They collect beginnings the way other people collect stamps. They have a drawer full of weird hobbies they tried for two weeks and then gently set down.

And the beautiful part? Nothing is wasted.

The novel you abandoned on page 73 taught you how to write a better first sentence. The half-knitted sweater taught your hands how to be patient. The garden that failed taught you when the frost actually comes in your town, not when the internet says it does.

We like to think of our lives as a single straight line, one arrow flying toward one target. But it's more like a river delta — fanning out, trying many paths to the sea. Some channels dry up. That's not tragedy. That's hydrology.

So if you have something unfinished right now — and you do, everyone does — consider not feeling guilty about it today. Consider thanking it instead.

Pick one unfinished thing in your mind. Just one.

Now ask: What did it give me, even unfinished? 

You might be surprised how much it already did.

---

What kind of unfinished thing lives on your shelf?
